region_name: Wilderness Coast: Shi Shi, Ozette, North Coast, South Coast, Kalaloch
summary: Olympic's Wilderness Coast is 73 miles of roadless beach, sea stacks, rope-and-ladder overland trails and tannin-dark creeks, split by the Quillayute River into the North Coast Route (Shi Shi to Rialto, ~35 mi, with the quota-limited Ozette Triangle and Cape Alava at its heart) and the South Coast Route (Third Beach to Oil City, 17 mi), plus easy day beaches at Second Beach, Rialto, Ruby Beach and Kalaloch. The defining mechanic is the tide: specific headlands pass only below set heights (Cape Johnson 4 ft with no overland trail, Diamond Rock 2 ft, Taylor Point cove 4.5 ft, Yellow Banks 5-6 ft), the Ozette, Goodman, Falls and Mosquito Creek fords want low tide, and bear canisters are mandatory everywhere because raccoons and bears patrol the camps. Elevation is trivial but pace is not - 1 mph over kelp-slick boulders is normal - so the coast rewards a tide table, a watch, gloves, water shoes, a canister and patience, and punishes day-hike gear and wishful timing. 2026 logistics matter: Mora Road to Rialto is closed for construction (NPS: to Oct 15; recreation.gov: to Nov 9), the US 101 Hoh River Bridge has multi-day closures that cut Ruby Beach and Kalaloch off from Forks, and a park-wide campfire ban was in force from August.

nodes.name: Neah Bay
nodes.description: The road ends in a fishing village wrapped around a harbor, where gulls argue on the pilings and the smell of salt and diesel hangs in the fog. This is Makah land; before any boot touches Shi Shi sand, a hiker stops here for the tribe's recreation pass.
nodes.scene_art_notes: Foreground: a weathered wooden sign and a pass booth window; midground: harbor with small fishing boats (white, red hulls) and a breakwater; sky: dithered light grey fog over dark green hills; landmark: Waadah Island humped beyond the harbor mouth. Palette: dark blue water, dark grey pilings, white gulls.

nodes.name: Shi Shi overnight parking (private lot)
nodes.description: Overnight cars may not stay at the trailhead, so backpackers leave them on a grassy yard about half a mile back down the road and drop cash in a box.
nodes.scene_art_notes: Foreground: a hand-lettered cardboard sign 'OVERNIGHT PARKING' (no real business name) and a lockbox; midground: rows of dusty cars on a lawn beside a house; sky: low grey; landmark: spruce wall at the yard's edge.

nodes.name: Shi Shi Beach Trailhead (Makah Reservation)
nodes.description: A small gravel lot by the fish hatchery, a pit toilet, and a trail that starts politely on boardwalk before the forest turns soft and sucking underfoot.
nodes.scene_art_notes: Foreground: trail post with a red-and-black target sign and a muddy boot print; midground: boardwalk entering dense Sitka spruce and salal; sky: thin grey strip through treetops; landmark: hatchery roof just visible. Palette: dark green, brown, light grey.

nodes.name: Shi Shi Beach access (bluff descent at park boundary)
nodes.description: The forest opens at the lip of a bluff and the whole bay appears at once: a long pale crescent of sand, white surf lines, and a fleet of sea stacks waiting at the far end. A steep, newly stepped path drops to the beach and into the national park.
nodes.scene_art_notes: Foreground: wooden steps with a handrail dropping off the bluff; midground: wide sand crescent with driftwood logs; sky: dithered light blue to white haze; landmark: Point of the Arches as dark jagged stacks on the far left horizon.

nodes.name: Shi Shi Beach (camp area, Petroleum Creek)

camp.reservation_or_quota: Wilderness permit required (Shi Shi is outside the Ozette quota zone). recreation.gov nightly cap shows 100 permits / 300 people (2026-10-08). NPS: up to ~250 campers on busy summer weekends.
camp.water: Petroleum Creek (south end of the camping area) and Willoughby Creek; tannin-stained; filter or boil (crypto and giardia present; iodine ineffective). Petroleum Creek can be hard to cross after heavy winter rain.
camp.notes: Fires only on open beach below the high-tide line, driftwood only, at least 10 ft from drift logs, max 3 ft across; never in forested sites. 2026: a park-wide Stage 2 campfire ban was in effect from Aug 7 (still listed Aug 26); status in October 2026 unconfirmed. Park-approved bear canister required for all food, garbage and scented items (hanging is not allowed; raccoons defeat hangs). Three pit toilets (south end of camps, behind the wooded sites on the south side of Petroleum Creek, and near Willoughby Creek). No overnight parking at the trailhead; Makah Recreation Pass required. Rangers often camp here and check permits and canisters (Jul 2026).

nodes.description: Tents freckle the drift logs and the forest edge for more than a mile. Petroleum Creek runs the color of strong tea across the sand, and the surf here is so loud it can wake a sleeper.
nodes.scene_art_notes: Foreground: a small tent and a blue bear canister on driftwood; midground: brown tannic creek fanning across sand; sky: sunset bands (light red, yellow, magenta dither) over sea; landmark: Point of the Arches stacks silhouetted black to the south.

nodes.name: Point of the Arches
nodes.description: A mile-long parade of sea stacks marches out into the Pacific, some pierced by arches the waves have bored straight through. At low tide the rocks are carpeted with sea stars and green anemones; at high tide the way south closes.
nodes.scene_art_notes: Foreground: tide pool with orange and purple sea stars (light red, magenta) and green anemones; midground: black rock arches with white foam; sky: pale yellow-to-light-cyan dither; landmark: the largest arch framing a bright patch of ocean.

nodes.name: Pocket beach below the overland trails (Father and Son view)
nodes.description: Between two muddy rope climbs lies a tiny hidden beach, and out in the swell stand two rocks, one tall and one small, like a parent walking with a child.
nodes.scene_art_notes: Foreground: frayed rope hanging down a muddy bluff; midground: tiny crescent of grey sand; sky: dithered grey-blue; landmark: Father and Son rocks (one big, one small black stack) offshore.

nodes.name: Seafield Creek

camp.reservation_or_quota: Ozette coast quota area (Yellow Banks to Point of the Arches): reservation required year-round; recreation.gov nightly limit 6 people (smallest on the coast; NPS max group size here is 6) (read from availability API 2026-10-08).
camp.water: Seafield Creek, tea-colored; best water is in slower beaver ponds above the log jam (not briny). Can run stagnant later in summer.
camp.notes: Fires only on open beach below the high-tide line, driftwood only, at least 10 ft from drift logs, max 3 ft across; never in forested sites. 2026: a park-wide Stage 2 campfire ban was in effect from Aug 7 (still listed Aug 26); status in October 2026 unconfirmed. Park-approved bear canister required for all food, garbage and scented items (hanging is not allowed; raccoons defeat hangs). NPS camp list shows no toilet (one 2026 trip report mentions a privy; unverified). A rope just north of the log jam leads to a windy bluff-top site.

nodes.description: A quiet beach with a log jam at the creek mouth and beaver ponds hidden just upstream. Few people come this far; the camp is small and the solitude is large.
nodes.scene_art_notes: Foreground: tumbled drift logs at a creek mouth; midground: a single tent on sand, a rope disappearing up the bluff to a hidden bench camp; sky: low fog bank (light grey dither); landmark: two distant cabins on the hill (no names).

nodes.name: North Side of Ozette River

camp.reservation_or_quota: Ozette coast quota area (Yellow Banks to Point of the Arches): reservation required year-round; recreation.gov nightly limit 16 people (read from availability API 2026-10-08).
camp.water: Ozette River is too brackish to filter near the mouth; fresh water 10-12 min up an overgrown path from the northernmost forest site, or carry from Seafield Creek (about 2 mi north).
camp.notes: Fires only on open beach below the high-tide line, driftwood only, at least 10 ft from drift logs, max 3 ft across; never in forested sites. 2026: a park-wide Stage 2 campfire ban was in effect from Aug 7 (still listed Aug 26); status in October 2026 unconfirmed. Park-approved bear canister required for all food, garbage and scented items (hanging is not allowed; raccoons defeat hangs). Camping here lets you ford the river at the next low tide instead of arriving on a rising one.

nodes.description: Tents sit at the edge of the beach grass where the Ozette River slides into the sea. The river water is brackish, so hikers walk to Seafield Creek or follow an overgrown path upriver to a small stream.
nodes.scene_art_notes: Foreground: tent and driftwood windbreak; midground: wide brown river mouth meeting surf; sky: evening light red/yellow bands; landmark: Cape Alava's islands to the south.

nodes.name: Ozette River ford
nodes.description: The outlet of Lake Ozette meets the ocean here, and the crossing changes with every tide: shin-deep at a good low, chest-deep and pushy at mid-tide, impassable after heavy rain.
nodes.scene_art_notes: Foreground: two hiking poles planted in brown water, boots tied to a pack; midground: river mouth with sandbar and breaking waves; sky: grey with a pale sun disc; landmark: dark spruce on both banks.

nodes.name: South Side of Ozette River

camp.reservation_or_quota: Ozette coast quota area (Yellow Banks to Point of the Arches): reservation required year-round; recreation.gov nightly limit 12 people (read from availability API 2026-10-08).
camp.water: River water is brackish near the mouth; fresh water is hard to reach on this side (go far upriver) - carry from Cape Alava.
camp.notes: Fires only on open beach below the high-tide line, driftwood only, at least 10 ft from drift logs, max 3 ft across; never in forested sites. 2026: a park-wide Stage 2 campfire ban was in effect from Aug 7 (still listed Aug 26); status in October 2026 unconfirmed. Park-approved bear canister required for all food, garbage and scented items (hanging is not allowed; raccoons defeat hangs). Only one really good site per a 2025 report. Camping is prohibited on the Ozette Indian Reservation between Cape Alava and this camp.

nodes.description: A handful of sites on the south bank of the river, where hikers bound north wait for the tide to fall before wading across.
nodes.scene_art_notes: Foreground: tent in shore pines; midground: river channel; sky: grey; landmark: sandbar at the river mouth.

nodes.name: Cape Alava

camp.reservation_or_quota: Ozette coast quota area (Yellow Banks to Point of the Arches): reservation required year-round; recreation.gov nightly limit 43 people (read from availability API 2026-10-08).
camp.water: Creek at Cape Alava; tannin-bitter but adequate in 2026; filter or boil.
camp.notes: Fires only on open beach below the high-tide line, driftwood only, at least 10 ft from drift logs, max 3 ft across; never in forested sites. 2026: a park-wide Stage 2 campfire ban was in effect from Aug 7 (still listed Aug 26); status in October 2026 unconfirmed. Little or no driftwood here in summer. Park-approved bear canister required for all food, garbage and scented items (hanging is not allowed; raccoons defeat hangs). Two upgraded privies (2026). A habituated black bear roamed the camp area in July 2026. Tskawahyah (Cannonball) Island is always closed to the public.

nodes.description: The westernmost point of the contiguous United States, where islands crowned with trees float offshore and sea lions bark through the night. Makah people lived here for at least two thousand years; part of their village lay buried by a mudslide for centuries until archaeologists uncovered it.
nodes.scene_art_notes: Foreground: tent and bear canister on sand; midground: kelp beds and a black bear nosing seaweed (small); sky: dithered fog lifting to light blue; landmark: Tskawahyah (Cannonball) Island and Ozette Island with tufts of trees.

nodes.name: Tskawahyah Island (Cannonball Island)
nodes.description: A round, tree-topped island that can be walked to at low tide, but must not be: it is closed to visitors out of respect for the Makah.
nodes.scene_art_notes: Foreground: sign post 'Closed'; midground: wet sand bar at low tide; sky: grey-blue; landmark: domed island with a fringe of trees.

nodes.name: Ahlstrom's Prairie
nodes.description: Halfway out the Cape Alava boardwalk the forest steps back to a wide, soggy meadow where a homesteader once grazed animals. Now only the wind and the sedges farm it.
nodes.scene_art_notes: Foreground: grey cedar boardwalk planks; midground: open boggy meadow (light green, brown) with a few shore pines; sky: wide dithered grey; landmark: dark forest wall around the clearing.

nodes.name: Cape Alava / Sand Point trail junction
nodes.description: A quarter mile from the ranger station the boardwalk forks: right for Cape Alava, left for Sand Point. Either way, the ocean is three miles off.
nodes.scene_art_notes: Foreground: wooden signpost with two arrows; midground: boardwalk splitting into the ferns; sky: none (canopy); landmark: giant cedar trunk.

nodes.name: Ozette Ranger Station Trailhead
nodes.description: At the north end of Lake Ozette, a small ranger station, a big parking lot, and an arched bridge over the river mark the start of two boardwalk trails to the sea.
nodes.scene_art_notes: Foreground: arched wooden footbridge; midground: ranger station cabin with brown siding; sky: soft grey; landmark: Lake Ozette's calm water through the trees.

nodes.name: Ozette Campground
nodes.description: Fifteen first-come sites beside Lake Ozette, handy for an early start; the campground often closes in winter when the lake floods it.
nodes.scene_art_notes: Foreground: picnic table; midground: lake shore; sky: grey; landmark: misty lake.

nodes.name: Wedding Rocks petroglyphs
nodes.description: On the boulders at the base of a rocky point, ancestors of the Makah pecked whales, faces and other figures into the stone, some of them centuries old. One whale lies so low that the high tide covers it.
nodes.scene_art_notes: Foreground: grey boulder with a carved orca outline and a round face (lines in white/light grey); midground: more boulders and kelp; sky: light cyan; landmark: the rocky headland.

nodes.name: Wedding Rocks (camp)

camp.reservation_or_quota: Ozette coast quota area (Yellow Banks to Point of the Arches): reservation required year-round; recreation.gov nightly limit 20 people (read from availability API 2026-10-08).
camp.water: Unreliable: the Wedding Rocks source typically dries later in summer; carry water from Cape Alava or Sand Point.
camp.notes: Campfires prohibited from the Wedding Rocks headland south to the headland north of Yellow Banks. Park-approved bear canister required for all food, garbage and scented items (hanging is not allowed; raccoons defeat hangs). Use the privies at Cape Alava or Sand Point, otherwise a cathole.

nodes.description: A small camp on the quiet stretch between Cape Alava and Sand Point, just past the petroglyph boulders. There is no water late in summer and no privy.
nodes.scene_art_notes: Foreground: tent tucked against salal; midground: rocky beach; sky: grey; landmark: petroglyph headland to the north.

nodes.name: Sand Point

camp.reservation_or_quota: Ozette coast quota area (Yellow Banks to Point of the Arches): reservation required year-round; recreation.gov nightly limit 100 (may be a system default cap rather than a true quota) (read from availability API 2026-10-08).
camp.water: Wish Creek ('Ozette tea'); can dry up later in summer - carry water if late season.
camp.notes: No campfires (closure from Wedding Rocks headland to north of Yellow Banks, due to past fire damage). Park-approved bear canister required for all food, garbage and scented items (hanging is not allowed; raccoons defeat hangs). Two privies (near the point and near Wish Creek).

nodes.description: A sandy spit with a grassy knob of rock at its tip, wide beaches on both sides, and Wish Creek tumbling out of the forest. Black bears sometimes forage in the seaweed here at dawn.
nodes.scene_art_notes: Foreground: two tents among drift logs; midground: broad pale beach curving south; sky: dawn light yellow over grey; landmark: the small rocky point (climbable knob) with wind-bent trees.

nodes.name: South Sand Point

camp.reservation_or_quota: Ozette coast quota area (Yellow Banks to Point of the Arches): reservation required year-round; recreation.gov nightly limit 50 people (read from availability API 2026-10-08).
camp.water: Small tannic creek; adequate in June 2026; typically dries later in summer - carry water.
camp.notes: No campfires. Park-approved bear canister required for all food, garbage and scented items (hanging is not allowed; raccoons defeat hangs). New privy (2025). Camping begins south of the Ericson's Bay trail.

nodes.description: About a mile south of Sand Point, a few sites hide in the forest above the beach, reached by buoys and ropes. A primitive trail slips inland from here to Lake Ozette.
nodes.scene_art_notes: Foreground: rope with fishing buoys hanging on a root ball; midground: forest campsites above sand; sky: grey; landmark: headland north of Yellow Banks to the south.

nodes.name: Ericson's Bay (Lake Ozette)

camp.reservation_or_quota: Ozette area permit required; recreation.gov nightly cap shows 100.
camp.water: Lake Ozette; filter or boil.
camp.notes: Fires in existing rings only, dead and down wood. Park-approved bear canister required for all food, garbage and scented items (hanging is not allowed; raccoons defeat hangs). Lake Ozette can kick up 1-2 ft waves; wear life jackets.

nodes.description: A lakeshore camp on the west side of Lake Ozette, reached by paddling about four miles or by a two-mile primitive trail from South Sand Point.
nodes.scene_art_notes: Foreground: canoe pulled up on a pebble shore; midground: calm grey lake; sky: soft overcast; landmark: forested lake islands.

nodes.name: Lake Ozette
nodes.description: Eight miles long and three wide, the largest unaltered natural lake in Washington lies just behind the coastal hills, still and dark under the fog.
nodes.scene_art_notes: Foreground: reeds; midground: wide flat lake (dark blue, light grey reflections); sky: layered fog; landmark: small forested islands.

nodes.name: Yellow Banks

camp.reservation_or_quota: Ozette coast quota area (Yellow Banks to Point of the Arches): reservation required year-round; recreation.gov nightly limit 12 people (read from availability API 2026-10-08). Recreation.gov notes 'no access via Rialto 7/8-11/9' (2026 Mora Road closure).
camp.water: Plentiful from creeks in spring (largest creek mid-beach).
camp.notes: Fires only on open beach below the high-tide line, driftwood only, at least 10 ft from drift logs, max 3 ft across; never in forested sites. 2026: a park-wide Stage 2 campfire ban was in effect from Aug 7 (still listed Aug 26); status in October 2026 unconfirmed. Park-approved bear canister required for all food, garbage and scented items (hanging is not allowed; raccoons defeat hangs). No privy; dig catholes in the forest. Sites: cobble beach above high tide, a 1-tent site marked by a buoy, 3 small sites ~100 ft up a hidden rope ~50 ft south of the main creek, and a larger bench north of the creek marked by buoys on a root ball (May 2026).

nodes.description: A mile-long beach under ochre bluffs, the last easy walking before the rocky miles to the south. Campsites are hard to find: a few on the cobbles, a few up ropes in the trees.
nodes.scene_art_notes: Foreground: yellow-brown clay bluff (yellow, brown dither); midground: long beach of cobbles and sand; sky: light grey; landmark: headland at each end of the beach.

nodes.name: Norwegian Memorial (Kayostla Beach)

camp.reservation_or_quota: Wilderness permit required (south of the Ozette quota zone); recreation.gov nightly cap 100. 'No access via Rialto 7/8-11/9' in 2026.
camp.water: Norwegian Creek about 0.7 mi south of the memorial (low tannin in June 2026); no water at the north cluster.
camp.notes: Fires only on open beach below the high-tide line, driftwood only, at least 10 ft from drift logs, max 3 ft across; never in forested sites. 2026: a park-wide Stage 2 campfire ban was in effect from Aug 7 (still listed Aug 26); status in October 2026 unconfirmed. Park-approved bear canister required for all food, garbage and scented items (hanging is not allowed; raccoons defeat hangs). Two clusters: one at the memorial (north end) and one 0.7 mi south flanking Norwegian Creek. In June 2026 the privy north of the creek was signed full; use the one south of the creek.

nodes.description: A memorial remembers the sailors of the Norwegian ship Prince Arthur, lost on this shore in 1903. Today the long sandy beach is one of the loveliest camps on the coast, with a clear creek in the woods.
nodes.scene_art_notes: Foreground: small white memorial obelisk on a grassy bank; midground: long sand beach with drift logs; sky: dithered pink-to-grey dusk; landmark: offshore rocks (Hand Rock, Foot Rock) in the haze.

nodes.name: Cedar Creek

camp.reservation_or_quota: Wilderness permit required; recreation.gov nightly cap 100. 'No access via Rialto 7/8-11/9' in 2026.
camp.water: Cedar Creek is pond-like above the beach and may take on tide water; collect where it flows onto the sand. Another small creek ~0.25 mi south. A good source is reported around mile 6 from Rialto.
camp.notes: Fires only on open beach below the high-tide line, driftwood only, at least 10 ft from drift logs, max 3 ft across; never in forested sites. 2026: a park-wide Stage 2 campfire ban was in effect from Aug 7 (still listed Aug 26); status in October 2026 unconfirmed. Park-approved bear canister required for all food, garbage and scented items (hanging is not allowed; raccoons defeat hangs). NPS lists a pit toilet but 2026 hikers could not find it and the camp KML shows none; nearest privy at Norwegian Memorial (~0.75 mi).

nodes.description: Forest sites on either side of a creek that pools behind the beach like a little pond. Many hikers call it their favorite camp on the north coast.
nodes.scene_art_notes: Foreground: tent pads under spruce; midground: still creek pond with a thin outflow over sand; sky: grey-blue; landmark: Coastie Head to the south.

nodes.name: Coastie Head
nodes.description: A rounded headland with a short, steep rope trail over its back and a jam of drift logs waiting at the bottom on the south side.
nodes.scene_art_notes: Foreground: knotted rope on a muddy slope; midground: drift log jam; sky: grey; landmark: Jagged Island offshore.

nodes.name: Saddle Rock
nodes.description: A low rocky point with a tiny overland path; at low tide most hikers simply pick their way around on slippery shelves.
nodes.scene_art_notes: Foreground: kelp-slick rock shelf; midground: tide pools; sky: grey; landmark: Sandy Island offshore.

nodes.name: Cape Johnson
nodes.description: The first big tidal choke point north of Rialto: a long, broken rock shelf with no overland trail. It can only be passed when the tide is low.
nodes.scene_art_notes: Foreground: barnacled boulders and a narrow wet ledge; midground: surf boiling into a gap; sky: dark grey squall; landmark: the cape's forested bulk.

nodes.name: Chilean Memorial

camp.reservation_or_quota: Wilderness permit required; recreation.gov showed 0 availability Oct 7 - Nov 9, 2026 (Mora Road/Rialto closure), reopening Nov 10.
camp.water: At least two flowing creeks on either side of the memorial (spring 2026).
camp.notes: Fires only on open beach below the high-tide line, driftwood only, at least 10 ft from drift logs, max 3 ft across; never in forested sites. 2026: a park-wide Stage 2 campfire ban was in effect from Aug 7 (still listed Aug 26); status in October 2026 unconfirmed. Park-approved bear canister required for all food, garbage and scented items (hanging is not allowed; raccoons defeat hangs). Privy is an open 'forest throne' up a short, treacherous scramble marked by buoys and a knotted rope ~30 ft left of the marker. The headland just south of the marker has a rope up-and-over; going around on the rocks is described as very dangerous.

nodes.description: A marker on the beach honors the crew of the schooner W. J. Pirrie, lost in 1920. Fast little creeks spill across the sand, and sea stacks stand offshore like a ruined castle.
nodes.scene_art_notes: Foreground: memorial plaque on a rock and a rope with buoys up a bluff (to the privy); midground: sandy cove; sky: dithered sunset light red; landmark: cluster of sea stacks.

nodes.name: Hole-in-the-Wall
nodes.description: A sea arch big enough to walk through at low tide, framing the ocean like a window. When the tide is in, a short steep path with a rope climbs over the top instead.
nodes.scene_art_notes: Foreground: wet sand with a reflection; midground: large black arch with surf behind; sky: light yellow late sun; landmark: sea stacks visible through the hole.

nodes.name: Hole-in-the-Wall (camp area)

camp.reservation_or_quota: Wilderness permit required; recreation.gov showed 0 availability Oct 7 - Nov 9, 2026 (Mora Road closure).
camp.water: Ellen Creek (south) and small creeks; filter or boil.
camp.notes: Fires only in existing fire rings on the beach, driftwood only (NPS Rialto page); 2026 fire ban caveat applies. Park-approved bear canister required for all food, garbage and scented items (hanging is not allowed; raccoons defeat hangs). Pit toilet just south of Hole-in-the-Wall near 'split rock'.

nodes.description: A busy camp area close to Rialto, with sites strung along the beach between Ellen Creek and the arch.
nodes.scene_art_notes: Foreground: tents among drift logs; midground: beach; sky: grey; landmark: the arch.

nodes.name: Ellen Creek
nodes.description: A small stream that fans across Rialto's gravel; usually a hop or a short wade. Leashed dogs may come this far and no farther.
nodes.scene_art_notes: Foreground: shallow brown creek on grey gravel; midground: drift logs; sky: grey; landmark: Hole-in-the-Wall headland ahead.

nodes.name: Rialto Beach Trailhead (Mora)
nodes.description: The road ends at a steep beach of round grey stones, piled with bleached logs as big as buses. James Island looms across the river mouth.
nodes.scene_art_notes: Foreground: giant bleached drift logs; midground: steep cobble beach and white surf; sky: storm grey with a bright gap; landmark: James Island across the Quillayute River.

nodes.name: Mora Campground
nodes.description: A forest campground beside the Quillayute River two miles from Rialto Beach, a common night-before stop for north coast hikers.
nodes.scene_art_notes: Foreground: picnic table and fire ring; midground: tall spruce and alder; sky: drizzle; landmark: river glimpse.

nodes.name: La Push
nodes.description: The Quileute village at the mouth of the Quillayute River, with a marina, a store and the trailheads to Second and Third Beach just up the road.
nodes.scene_art_notes: Foreground: fishing boats in a small marina; midground: village roofs; sky: grey; landmark: James Island.

nodes.name: Forks
nodes.description: The last real town before the coast, a timber town with groceries and gas where hikers stock up on the way to Rialto, La Push and Oil City.
nodes.scene_art_notes: Foreground: town sign; midground: timber-town main street; sky: grey drizzle; landmark: logging truck.

nodes.name: Second Beach Trailhead
nodes.description: A short trail starts on Quileute land, climbs a little rise through big trees, then drops down a crib staircase toward the sound of surf.
nodes.scene_art_notes: Foreground: kiosk with a mossy roof; midground: trail into huge spruce; sky: none; landmark: red-and-black overland target on a tree.

nodes.name: Second Beach

camp.reservation_or_quota: Wilderness permit required; recreation.gov nightly cap shows 100 (people cap 300 on some dates).
camp.water: Several freshwater creeks flow across the sand; filter or boil.
camp.notes: Fires only on open beach below the high-tide line, driftwood only, at least 10 ft from drift logs, max 3 ft across; never in forested sites. 2026: a park-wide Stage 2 campfire ban was in effect from Aug 7 (still listed Aug 26); status in October 2026 unconfirmed. Park-approved bear canister required for all food, garbage and scented items (hanging is not allowed; raccoons defeat hangs). Surrounded north and south by headlands that cannot be passed at any tide; Second Beach is a dead end, not part of the South Coast Route.

nodes.description: A sheltered beach between two headlands that can never be rounded, with sea stacks standing in a line offshore and an arch at the north end that moans in the wind. It is one of the easiest overnights in the park, and one of the busiest.
nodes.scene_art_notes: Foreground: kids' driftwood fort and a tent; midground: wide flat sand reflecting the sky; sky: sunset bands (light red, yellow, magenta); landmark: Crying Lady Rock and the Quillayute Needles as black silhouettes.

nodes.name: Crying Lady Rock
nodes.description: A tall sea stack at the south end of Second Beach whose shape, people say, looks like a woman bent in sorrow.
nodes.scene_art_notes: Foreground: wet sand; midground: tall stack with a bowed silhouette; sky: fog; landmark: the stack itself.

nodes.name: Quillayute Needles
nodes.description: A row of slender rock spires offshore, part of a wildlife refuge where seabirds nest out of reach.
nodes.scene_art_notes: Foreground: surf; midground: needle-thin stacks; sky: light cyan; landmark: seabirds as white dots.

nodes.name: Third Beach Trailhead
nodes.description: A roadside lot with room for about twenty cars, and a wide old roadbed that wanders through hemlock and spruce before plunging toward the beach.
nodes.scene_art_notes: Foreground: small parking lot and privy; midground: wide trail into tall hemlocks; sky: drizzle grey; landmark: trail sign 'Third Beach 1.4'.

nodes.name: Third Beach

camp.reservation_or_quota: Wilderness permit required; recreation.gov nightly cap 100 (a 2026 report says 99 permits/night).
camp.water: Creek at the trail's arrival point; tannic; filter or boil.
camp.notes: Fires only on open beach below the high-tide line, driftwood only, at least 10 ft from drift logs, max 3 ft across; never in forested sites. 2026: a park-wide Stage 2 campfire ban was in effect from Aug 7 (still listed Aug 26); status in October 2026 unconfirmed. Park-approved bear canister required for all food, garbage and scented items (hanging is not allowed; raccoons defeat hangs). Privy up a short side trail on the south side of the creek (across a driftwood scramble). Very busy on weekends; late arrivals end up low on the sand and can be flooded at high tide.

nodes.description: A mile-long curve of sand on Strawberry Bay, closed off by Teahwhit Head to the north and Taylor Point to the south, where a waterfall drops off the cliff straight into the sea.
nodes.scene_art_notes: Foreground: log-choked creek mouth with a tent; midground: sweeping sand bay; sky: dithered light blue; landmark: thin white waterfall pouring off Taylor Point's dark cliff.

nodes.name: Teahwhit Head
nodes.description: The cliff wall between Second and Third Beach. It cannot be rounded at shore level at any tide.
nodes.scene_art_notes: Foreground: surf; midground: sheer cliff into the sea; sky: grey; landmark: arch-pierced headland.

nodes.name: Taylor Point overland trail (north ladders)
nodes.description: At the south end of Third Beach, a red-and-black target nailed to a tree marks the way up: four or five ladders and ropes climbing a muddy bluff into the forest.
nodes.scene_art_notes: Foreground: wooden ladder with a rope beside it; midground: steep muddy bluff with roots; sky: grey slot above trees; landmark: circular red-and-black target sign.

nodes.name: Cove south of Taylor Point
nodes.description: The overland trail comes back down stairs into a little rocky cove with a freshwater stream. At tides above about four and a half feet the cove floods.
nodes.scene_art_notes: Foreground: stairs ending on rocks; midground: small cove with a stream; sky: light grey; landmark: Taylor Point cliff behind.

nodes.name: Scott's Bluff
nodes.description: A blunt bluff guarding Scott Creek. The rope-assisted path over it is short but slick, and in spring 2026 its north ladder washed out, leaving only the rope.
nodes.scene_art_notes: Foreground: muddy chute with a thick rope; midground: barnacled boulders below; sky: grey; landmark: bluff crowned with spruce.

nodes.name: Scott Creek

camp.reservation_or_quota: Wilderness permit required; recreation.gov nightly cap 100.
camp.water: Scott Creek; reach past the driftwood to avoid brackish water at high tide.
camp.notes: Fires only on open beach below the high-tide line, driftwood only, at least 10 ft from drift logs, max 3 ft across; never in forested sites. 2026: a park-wide Stage 2 campfire ban was in effect from Aug 7 (still listed Aug 26); status in October 2026 unconfirmed. Park-approved bear canister required for all food, garbage and scented items (hanging is not allowed; raccoons defeat hangs). NPS route page says three small sites and no privy, but the park camp map shows a privy; a covered privy was flagged closed in June 2026 and reported usable in Sept 2026. Camp on the beach only - headland sites are signed closed for wildlife (cougar notice at trailhead, June 2026). A burned trash pile was reported here in July 2026.

nodes.description: A small camp where Scott Creek meets the beach, with good sand above the tide line and the Giants Graveyard of sea stacks just down the shore.
nodes.scene_art_notes: Foreground: tent on sand by a creek; midground: shed-like privy at the forest edge; sky: dawn light; landmark: Giants Graveyard stacks to the south.

nodes.name: Giants Graveyard
nodes.description: A crowd of dark sea stacks scattered offshore like the tumbled tombstones of giants, half hidden in fog.
nodes.scene_art_notes: Foreground: wet sand with gull tracks; midground: many jagged black stacks in white surf; sky: thick light grey fog dither; landmark: the stacks.

nodes.name: Strawberry Point

camp.reservation_or_quota: Wilderness permit required; recreation.gov nightly cap 100.
camp.water: None; carry from Scott Creek (~1.3 mi north) or Jackson Creek just past Toleak (~1.2 mi south).
camp.notes: Fires only on open beach below the high-tide line, driftwood only, at least 10 ft from drift logs, max 3 ft across; never in forested sites. 2026: a park-wide Stage 2 campfire ban was in effect from Aug 7 (still listed Aug 26); status in October 2026 unconfirmed. Park-approved bear canister required for all food, garbage and scented items (hanging is not allowed; raccoons defeat hangs). No privy.

nodes.description: A low sandy point with wide tide pools and forested sites behind it. There is no fresh water here, so hikers fill up at Scott Creek or Toleak.
nodes.scene_art_notes: Foreground: vast tide pool flats with purple shore crabs; midground: sandy point with tents in the trees; sky: clear light blue; landmark: Toleak Point stacks ahead.

nodes.name: Toleak Point

camp.reservation_or_quota: Wilderness permit required; recreation.gov nightly cap 100.
camp.water: Jackson Creek, just south of the point (closest reliable source); climb over the driftwood and go a bit upstream.
camp.notes: Fires only on open beach below the high-tide line, driftwood only, at least 10 ft from drift logs, max 3 ft across; never in forested sites. 2026: a park-wide Stage 2 campfire ban was in effect from Aug 7 (still listed Aug 26); status in October 2026 unconfirmed. Park-approved bear canister required for all food, garbage and scented items (hanging is not allowed; raccoons defeat hangs). Privies on both sides of the point; the south one was full in Sept 2026. Several dead whales were stranded near Toleak through summer 2026 (smell depends on wind).

nodes.description: The favorite camp of the south coast: a point of sand and rock studded with sea stacks, eagles in the spruce, and long sunsets. Forest shelves behind the beach hold the snuggest sites.
nodes.scene_art_notes: Foreground: tent on a forest shelf; midground: point of sand and sea stacks; sky: brilliant sunset (light red, yellow, magenta); landmark: bald eagle on a snag.

nodes.name: Jackson Creek
nodes.description: A strong little creek pushing through a jam of drift logs just south of Toleak Point; the best water for miles.
nodes.scene_art_notes: Foreground: water filter bag hanging on a log; midground: clear brown creek; sky: grey; landmark: Toleak's sea stacks.

nodes.name: Goodman Creek overland trail (north end)
nodes.description: Past a pair of natural arches the beach ends at cliffs. A ladder and rope lead up into the forest for the long detour around Goodman Creek's mouth.
nodes.scene_art_notes: Foreground: ladder against a bluff with hanging buoys as trail markers; midground: natural arch; sky: grey; landmark: a stranded whale skeleton on the beach (2026, optional).

nodes.name: Falls Creek ford
nodes.description: A creek crossing deep in the forest, with a waterfall just upstream. Usually ankle-deep, but at high tides the ocean pushes up the channel and the water can reach the waist.
nodes.scene_art_notes: Foreground: wading shoes on a gravel bar; midground: knee-deep creek; sky: none (canopy); landmark: small waterfall in a mossy ravine.

nodes.name: Goodman Creek ford
nodes.description: The bigger of the two forest fords, usually ankle- to knee-deep; after heavy rain it can be impossible.
nodes.scene_art_notes: Foreground: two poles in moving water; midground: wide creek with logs; sky: green canopy; landmark: mossy maples.

nodes.name: Goodman Creek overland trail (south end)
nodes.description: Ropes and steps lower hikers back to the sand for an easy stretch of lonely beach toward Mosquito Creek.
nodes.scene_art_notes: Foreground: rope down a slope; midground: long empty beach; sky: light blue; landmark: Alexander Island offshore.

nodes.name: Mosquito Creek ford
nodes.description: Mosquito Creek fans out across the beach; at low tide it can be crossed barefoot in the sand, at higher tides it is knee-deep or worse.
nodes.scene_art_notes: Foreground: bare feet in shallow water; midground: braided creek across sand; sky: grey; landmark: wooded bluff with camp sign.

nodes.name: Mosquito Creek

camp.reservation_or_quota: Wilderness permit required; recreation.gov nightly cap 100, but the system showed 0 available Oct 12-15, 2026 (cause not stated; likely the Diamond Rock tide window).
camp.water: Mosquito Creek, a short walk along the trail; good water.
camp.notes: Fires only on open beach below the high-tide line, driftwood only, at least 10 ft from drift logs, max 3 ft across; never in forested sites. 2026: a park-wide Stage 2 campfire ban was in effect from Aug 7 (still listed Aug 26); status in October 2026 unconfirmed. Park-approved bear canister required for all food, garbage and scented items (hanging is not allowed; raccoons defeat hangs). Four main campsites and a privy up the bluff trail south of the creek; limited beach camping. Travel north from Oil City requires a tide of 2 ft or lower at Diamond Rock.

nodes.description: Four main sites on a wooded bluff above the creek, with a bench someone built and a view of whales spouting off Alexander Island. Despite the name, the sea breeze usually keeps bugs away.
nodes.scene_art_notes: Foreground: hand-built log bench; midground: bluff-top tent among spruce; sky: dusk with whale spouts (white dots); landmark: Alexander Island.

nodes.name: Alexander Island
nodes.description: A rocky island off Mosquito Creek where whales are often seen spouting at sunset.
nodes.scene_art_notes: Foreground: beach grass on the bluff; midground: grey sea; sky: dusk light red; landmark: dark island with white spout plumes beside it.

nodes.name: Hoh Head (overland trail high point)
nodes.description: A great forested headland that no one should try to round on the beach. The 3.5-mile overland trail over it is the longest on the coast: muddy, brushy, and full of ropes and ladders, with peeks of ocean through the trees.
nodes.scene_art_notes: Foreground: mud, skunk cabbage (yellow), a rope; midground: dense forest; sky: grey glimpses of sea through trunks; landmark: cliff edge with a sweep of ocean far below.

nodes.name: Jefferson Cove
nodes.description: A small sandy cove at the foot of weathered stairs and a ladder. At high tide the waves run right up to the cliff, leaving room for only a single forest campsite.
nodes.scene_art_notes: Foreground: steep wooden stairs and ladder; midground: sandy cove with surf to the cliff; sky: grey; landmark: Diamond Rock to the south.

nodes.name: Diamond Rock
nodes.description: A quarter mile of barnacled boulders wraps around this point. It can only be passed at a tide of two feet or lower, and some weeks the daylight tides never fall that far.
nodes.scene_art_notes: Foreground: barnacle-crusted boulders (dark grey, white specks) and slippery kelp; midground: boulder field against a cliff with waves; sky: dawn grey; landmark: diamond-shaped stack.

nodes.name: Hoh River mouth (beach camp)

camp.reservation_or_quota: Wilderness permit required; listed on recreation.gov as a hidden 'Hoh River Mouth' zone; booking details unverified.
camp.water: Hoh River is glacial and silty near the mouth; small creeks; filter or boil.
camp.notes: Fires only on open beach below the high-tide line, driftwood only, at least 10 ft from drift logs, max 3 ft across; never in forested sites. 2026: a park-wide Stage 2 campfire ban was in effect from Aug 7 (still listed Aug 26); status in October 2026 unconfirmed. Park-approved bear canister required for all food, garbage and scented items (hanging is not allowed; raccoons defeat hangs). No toilets; bury waste, urinate below the high-tide line. Space can be scarce in summer.

nodes.description: Where the Hoh River, born on Mount Olympus's glaciers, finally meets the sea. Hikers camp among the drift logs; the far bank is Hoh tribal land and the river cannot be forded.
nodes.scene_art_notes: Foreground: tent tucked in a nest of bleached logs; midground: wide grey-green river mouth; sky: grey; landmark: Destruction Island far to the south.

nodes.name: Oil City Trailhead
nodes.description: At the end of a long road beside the Hoh, a short forest path follows the river bank toward the ocean. Oil seeps in the hills once lured prospectors who hoped for a boom town; only the name stayed.
nodes.scene_art_notes: Foreground: trailhead privy and sign; midground: path into alder and spruce along a river; sky: grey; landmark: Hoh River glinting.

nodes.name: Ruby Beach Trailhead
nodes.description: A highway pullout on a bluff, two vault toilets, and a short path down through spruce to a beach heaped with silver drift logs.
nodes.scene_art_notes: Foreground: guardrail and parking stripe; midground: short trail into spruce; sky: fog; landmark: Abbey Island visible below.

nodes.name: Ruby Beach
nodes.description: Cedar Creek pools behind a barricade of bleached logs, and Abbey Island rises from the sand like a tree-topped fortress. At low tide the stacks are dressed in sea stars.
nodes.scene_art_notes: Foreground: drift log tangle (light grey, white) and a creek pool; midground: dark sand with tide pools; sky: pink sunset dither; landmark: Abbey Island and sea stacks.

nodes.name: Abbey Island
nodes.description: A forested sea stack at Ruby Beach that can be reached across the sand only at low tide.
nodes.scene_art_notes: Foreground: wet sand; midground: steep island with trees; sky: grey; landmark: island.

nodes.name: Destruction Island
nodes.description: A flat island a few miles offshore with an old lighthouse tower, visible from Ruby Beach and Kalaloch on clear days.
nodes.scene_art_notes: Foreground: beach grass; midground: sea; sky: clear; landmark: low island with a white lighthouse tower.

nodes.name: Beach 4 Trailhead
nodes.description: A short path and steps lead down from the highway to one of the best tide-pool shelves on the coast.
nodes.scene_art_notes: Foreground: stairs; midground: sandstone shelf with pools; sky: light cyan; landmark: layered cliff.

nodes.name: Beach 4 tide pools
nodes.description: At low tide a flat shelf of rock appears, full of pools where sea stars and green and pink anemones wait for the water to return.
nodes.scene_art_notes: Foreground: tide pool with ochre and purple sea stars and green anemones; midground: tilted rock shelf; sky: bright light blue; landmark: sea stack offshore.

nodes.name: Kalaloch
nodes.description: A cluster of cabins, a store and a campground on the bluff above a long beach. Beach camping is not allowed south of the Hoh; nights here are spent in the campgrounds.
nodes.scene_art_notes: Foreground: rustic cabins on a bluff; midground: wide beach with logs; sky: dusk; landmark: Kalaloch Rocks offshore.

nodes.name: Kalaloch Campground
nodes.description: A big year-round campground on the bluff above the sea, reservable in summer.
nodes.scene_art_notes: Foreground: picnic table; midground: wind-sculpted spruce; sky: grey; landmark: the ocean beyond the bluff.

nodes.name: Tree of Life (Kalaloch)
nodes.description: A Sitka spruce that hangs over a little ravine where the soil has washed out from under it, gripping both sides with bare roots. Storms in early 2025 dropped it about five feet; it may not last.
nodes.scene_art_notes: Foreground: sand and a trickle of creek; midground: spruce suspended above a cave of roots (brown tangles); sky: grey; landmark: the tree.

nodes.name: South Beach Campground
nodes.description: A simple first-come campground on the bluff just south of Kalaloch, open late spring to early fall.
nodes.scene_art_notes: Foreground: RVs and tents on grass; midground: driftwood; sky: grey; landmark: ocean.

segments.snow_free_typical: year-round (no snow; winter storms, high tides and swollen creeks are the seasonal limits)
segments.notes: Overnight hikers drop packs at the trailhead, then park about 0.6 mi back at a private yard and walk the road. 2026 reports: $20/night cash in a lockbox (older info: $10/day).

segments.snow_free_typical: year-round (no snow; winter storms, high tides and swollen creeks are the seasonal limits)
segments.notes: On Makah Reservation land until the park boundary at the bluff. First ~1 mi rehabilitated with boardwalks and bridges; second mile chronically deep mud (social paths skirt the worst, 2026). Bluff descent now has stairs and a railing (Aug 2026). Gain/loss estimated (WTA lists 200 ft gain, high point 200 ft).

segments.snow_free_typical: year-round (no snow; winter storms, high tides and swollen creeks are the seasonal limits)
segments.notes: Easy sand walking south; Petroleum Creek marks the start of the main camping area. No tidal restriction on Shi Shi Beach itself (Jul 2026 report). Petroleum Creek can be hard to cross after heavy winter rain.

segments.snow_free_typical: year-round (no snow; winter storms, high tides and swollen creeks are the seasonal limits)
segments.notes: Sand then rock toward the stacks; tide pools best below about +1 ft. Going around Point of the Arches and south requires a falling or low tide.

segments.snow_free_typical: year-round (no snow; winter storms, high tides and swollen creeks are the seasonal limits)
segments.notes: Hardest stretch of the Olympic coast. ~0.5 mi of rock from the Arches to the first overland (0.4 mi), then a 0.7 mi overland; both climb ~250 ft bluffs on eroded rope-assisted slopes, overgrown on top with logs to straddle or crawl under and an eroding edge. NPS lists multiple tidal restrictions of 4-6 ft between Point of the Arches and Seafield Creek; a 2026 party following the Custom Correct map needed 4 ft or lower in the first couple of miles. June 2026: a descent rope ended ~25 ft above the beach (paracord extension). Expect under 1 mph. Distance from 2026 trip reports (Seafield to Arches 3.7 mi total).

segments.snow_free_typical: year-round (no snow; winter storms, high tides and swollen creeks are the seasonal limits)
segments.notes: From the pocket beach a 0.1 mi overland with the steepest ascent and descent of the three, then a boulder field, then ~1.5 mi of mostly sand to Seafield Creek. Gain/loss not measured.

segments.snow_free_typical: year-round (no snow; winter storms, high tides and swollen creeks are the seasonal limits)
segments.notes: Mostly beach. A short pinch about 0.5 mi north of the Ozette River needs about 6 ft or lower (Custom Correct map, per July 2026 report; not on the NPS list). Above that, scramble the boulders or dash between waves.

segments.snow_free_typical: year-round (no snow; winter storms, high tides and swollen creeks are the seasonal limits)
segments.notes: Approach to the ford at the river mouth.

segments.snow_free_typical: year-round (no snow; winter storms, high tides and swollen creeks are the seasonal limits)
segments.notes: Ford only near low tide (2-3 hours either side is common practice). Shin-deep at low tide (Jun 2026); rib-cage deep at mid-tide (Aug 2026). May be impassable in shoulder seasons, winter and after heavy rain (NPS).

segments.snow_free_typical: year-round (no snow; winter storms, high tides and swollen creeks are the seasonal limits)
segments.notes: Crosses the Ozette Indian Reservation (Makah) where camping is prohibited. NPS tidal restriction 0.7 mi south of the Ozette River: two pinches at 5 ft and 4 ft. Distance from 2026 trip reports (Ozette TH to Seafield via Cape Alava ~7.5 mi; guide service lists 2.3 mi Ozette River to Cape Alava).

segments.snow_free_typical: year-round (no snow; winter storms, high tides and swollen creeks are the seasonal limits)
segments.notes: Cape Alava Trail: cedar boardwalk and stairs, very slick when wet; some rotten boards with exposed nails (wear closed-toe shoes). Length from NPS trail GIS; gain/loss from USGS DEM.

segments.snow_free_typical: year-round (no snow; winter storms, high tides and swollen creeks are the seasonal limits)
segments.notes: Boardwalk through forest and the open prairie. Length from NPS trail GIS; gain/loss from USGS DEM.

segments.snow_free_typical: year-round (no snow; winter storms, high tides and swollen creeks are the seasonal limits)
segments.notes: Crosses the Ozette River on an arched footbridge; shared by both legs of the Ozette Loop.

segments.snow_free_typical: year-round (no snow; winter storms, high tides and swollen creeks are the seasonal limits)
segments.notes: Sand Point Trail: about half boardwalk, half gravel; several boards loose or missing (2025-2026). Near the beach the trail splits; left is the direct way to the camps and privy. Length from NPS trail GIS; gain/loss from USGS DEM.

segments.snow_free_typical: year-round (no snow; winter storms, high tides and swollen creeks are the seasonal limits)
segments.notes: Beach with rock, kelp and downed trees to climb over and under. Two pinch points between Cape Alava and Sand Point have short high-tide overland routes (heights not published by NPS). Distance estimated from coordinates, consistent with the NPS 9.2 mi loop total.

segments.snow_free_typical: year-round (no snow; winter storms, high tides and swollen creeks are the seasonal limits)
segments.notes: Petroglyphs are on boulders around the base of the headland; some are covered at high tide. Do not touch or chalk them.

segments.snow_free_typical: year-round (no snow; winter storms, high tides and swollen creeks are the seasonal limits)
segments.notes: Rocky, slow beach; a 2026 party needed the overland route at the point north of Sand Point once the tide came in. Distance estimated from coordinates (loop total 9.2 mi).

segments.snow_free_typical: year-round (no snow; winter storms, high tides and swollen creeks are the seasonal limits)
segments.notes: Wide easy sand (0.7-0.9 mi depending on where you hit the beach).

segments.snow_free_typical: year-round (no snow; winter storms, high tides and swollen creeks are the seasonal limits)
segments.notes: Primitive trail inland to Lake Ozette, start marked by a brown PVC pipe; some brush and blowdown but easy to follow (Jun 2026). Length from NPS trail GIS; gain/loss from USGS DEM.

segments.snow_free_typical: year-round (no snow; winter storms, high tides and swollen creeks are the seasonal limits)
segments.notes: NPS tidal restriction 4.9 mi south of the Ozette TH (the headland north of Yellow Banks): 5 ft or lower. Campfire closure ends at this headland.

segments.snow_free_typical: year-round (no snow; winter storms, high tides and swollen creeks are the seasonal limits)
segments.notes: The 'purgatory' stretch: about 2 mi of loose rock and tidal shelves south of Yellow Banks, then a mile-long headland that needs 6 ft or lower (NPS: 7.9 mi south of the Ozette TH, 6 ft). No mandatory overland trails in this section (Jan 2025). Allow most of a day (6 h for ~6 mi in Jun 2026). Distance per Oregon Hikers mile log; others report 4-5 mi.

segments.snow_free_typical: year-round (no snow; winter storms, high tides and swollen creeks are the seasonal limits)
segments.notes: Along Kayostla Beach past the Norwegian Creek camps, then around Norwegian Head (0.09 mi way trail over the top in NPS GIS for higher tides). Distance uncertain: straight-line ~1.0 mi, Oregon Hikers ~2.0 mi; a 2026 party walked ~0.75 mi each way from Cedar Creek to the Norwegian Creek privy.

segments.snow_free_typical: year-round (no snow; winter storms, high tides and swollen creeks are the seasonal limits)
segments.notes: Rock and sand to Coastie Head. Distance estimated from coordinates.

segments.snow_free_typical: year-round (no snow; winter storms, high tides and swollen creeks are the seasonal limits)
segments.notes: Rope up-and-over Coastie Head (0.11 mi in NPS GIS), in good condition May 2026; careful descending toward the drift-log jam on the south side. Distance estimated from coordinates.

segments.snow_free_typical: year-round (no snow; winter storms, high tides and swollen creeks are the seasonal limits)
segments.notes: Includes the 'big bulbous headland before Cape Johnson'. NPS tidal restriction 5.1 mi north of Rialto TH: 5.5 ft or lower. Saddle Rock has a 0.06 mi way trail. Distance estimated from coordinates and the 20 mi route total.

segments.snow_free_typical: year-round (no snow; winter storms, high tides and swollen creeks are the seasonal limits)
segments.notes: Cape Johnson: NPS tidal restriction 4.3 mi north of Rialto TH, 4 ft or lower, and NO overland trail - one section goes out and around on seaweed-covered rock. In Jul 2025 hikers saw a packed tent nearly swept away near here.

segments.snow_free_typical: year-round (no snow; winter storms, high tides and swollen creeks are the seasonal limits)
segments.notes: Mostly headland rock-hopping, easier at low tide. NPS tidal restriction 2.4 mi north of Rialto TH: 5 ft or lower. The small headland immediately south of the Chilean Memorial marker has a rope up-and-over; going around it on the rocks is described as very dangerous with a pack.

segments.snow_free_typical: year-round (no snow; winter storms, high tides and swollen creeks are the seasonal limits)
segments.notes: Walk through the arch at low tide; at higher tide use the short steep overland trail (0.06 mi in NPS GIS) with a rope on the south side (north side trickier, Jan 2025). NPS does not publish a tide height for the arch.

segments.snow_free_typical: year-round (no snow; winter storms, high tides and swollen creeks are the seasonal limits)
segments.notes: Camps strung between Ellen Creek and the arch; busy with day hikers.

segments.snow_free_typical: year-round (no snow; winter storms, high tides and swollen creeks are the seasonal limits)
segments.notes: Steep cobble beach; at higher tides you are pushed onto loose upper-beach stones. Ellen Creek is a short wade or hop. Leashed pets allowed only to Ellen Creek.

segments.snow_free_typical: year-round (no snow; winter storms, high tides and swollen creeks are the seasonal limits)
segments.notes: Mora Road beyond Mora Campground is closed to vehicles, bikes AND pedestrians for construction July 8 - Oct 15, 2026 (NPS; recreation.gov camp names say through Nov 9). When open, overflow parking near the campground dump station is 1.8 mi from the trailhead.

segments.snow_free_typical: year-round (no snow; winter storms, high tides and swollen creeks are the seasonal limits)
segments.notes: No way across the Quillayute River on foot near the mouth: connecting the South and North Coast (e.g., on the Pacific Northwest Trail) means a road walk, shuttle or hitchhike via La Push Road and Mora Road (OSRM road distance; ~18 min drive). Mora Road closed to pedestrians in 2026 construction window.

segments.snow_free_typical: year-round (no snow; winter storms, high tides and swollen creeks are the seasonal limits)
segments.notes: Starts on the Quileute Reservation; park boundary at the top of the rise; crib staircase down to the beach. Length from NPS GIS; gain/loss from USGS DEM (NPS: ~200 ft descent).

segments.snow_free_typical: year-round (no snow; winter storms, high tides and swollen creeks are the seasonal limits)
segments.notes: Wide old roadbed for about a mile, then a steep, muddy, lightly switchbacked chute and a driftwood pile to the sand. NPS lists ~240-270 ft of descent.

segments.snow_free_typical: year-round (no snow; winter storms, high tides and swollen creeks are the seasonal limits)
segments.notes: Walk south along Third Beach past the waterfall that pours off Taylor Point (Strawberry Bay Falls). Teahwhit Head (north) and Taylor Point cannot be rounded at shore level. Distance estimated from coordinates.

segments.snow_free_typical: year-round (no snow; winter storms, high tides and swollen creeks are the seasonal limits)
segments.notes: Taylor Point overland: 4-5 low-angle ladders with ropes up the north side, about 1.25 mi in forest, then a steep, sometimes muddy descent with many stairs (newer steps reported 2026). Ladders reported in great condition Sept 2026. Length per NPS (GIS line 0.94 mi); gain/loss from USGS DEM.

segments.snow_free_typical: year-round (no snow; winter storms, high tides and swollen creeks are the seasonal limits)
segments.notes: The small rocky cove at the foot of the Taylor descent may be underwater above 4.5 ft (NPS: 3.0 mi south of Third Beach TH). A short, steep, loose bypass trail goes around the point at high tide.

segments.snow_free_typical: year-round (no snow; winter storms, high tides and swollen creeks are the seasonal limits)
segments.notes: Scott's Bluff overland: short, rope-assisted, essentially a muddy slide; the north-side ladder washed out in spring 2026 leaving a rope. Rounding the bluff on the rocks instead needs about +1 ft or lower and still involves barnacled boulders (trip reports; not an NPS figure). Length from NPS GIS; gain/loss from USGS DEM.

segments.snow_free_typical: year-round (no snow; winter storms, high tides and swollen creeks are the seasonal limits)
segments.notes: NPS tidal restriction just south of Scott Creek (4.25 mi south of Third Beach TH), passable at 4 ft or lower, extending around the arching beach toward Strawberry Point. Hikers found it impassable by mid-afternoon ahead of a 5:30 pm high tide (Jun 2026). Giants Graveyard sea stacks offshore.

segments.snow_free_typical: year-round (no snow; winter storms, high tides and swollen creeks are the seasonal limits)
segments.notes: Sea-level walking on sand and rock. NPS gives ~2.4 mi from Scott Creek to Toleak Point.

hazards.name: Cape Johnson: 4 ft and no overland trail
hazards.season: Year-round; worst in fall-winter storms when surge lifts tides above prediction
hazards.real_world: NPS lists a 4 ft restriction 4.3 mi north of Rialto with no headland trail. Hikers go out and around on seaweed-covered rock. A packed tent was nearly swept off the beach here in July 2025.
hazards.game_event_idea: Your watch says 1:40 pm; the tide table says 3.6 ft now, rising to 8 ft by 6. Options: (A) Go now, fast - success 80% with trekking poles and good shoes, 55% in trail runners; failure = soaked, dropped item, sprained ankle (slows next day). (B) Wait on the high beach for the evening low (need extra food/layers; adds a night if after dark without a headlamp). (C) Turn back to Chilean Memorial and try at dawn (requires flexible permit - in quota areas you must explain to a ranger). (D) Above 4.5 ft the game forbids A and narrates why.

hazards.name: Diamond Rock: the 2-foot gate
hazards.season: Worst Sept-Oct and March when daylight lows stay above 2 ft for days; best May-Aug mornings
hazards.real_world: Passable only at 2 ft or lower; may be impassable for whole days. In 2026 the daylight lows of Oct 12-15 were +2.2 to +3.9 ft while the minus tides fell after dark - recreation.gov showed Mosquito Creek permits unavailable those nights. A 2025 pair squeezed around at a rising ~5 ft tide, waves to mid-thigh, and called it the most dangerous moment of their trip.
hazards.game_event_idea: At Jefferson Cove the morning low is +2.8 ft. Options: (A) Scramble the boulders anyway - 50% success, else knocked down (lose an item, cold and wet, 10% injury). (B) Wait for the -0.6 ft low at 8:28 pm with a headlamp - 85% success with headlamp + spare batteries, 40% without. (C) Wait a whole day for a better tide (needs an extra food day and a campsite above a 10 ft night tide). (D) Retreat over Hoh Head and exit Third Beach (two more days).

hazards.name: Trapped between headlands by the rising tide
hazards.season: Year-round; storm surge in fall-spring raises water above predictions
hazards.real_world: NPS: tides can trap hikers below cliffs and people have died trying to beat the tide. The safest time to round a headland is within 1-2 hours before low tide; avoid rounding on an incoming tide. In 2021 two hikers at Hoh Head climbed 150 ft up a ledge to escape the tide and were hoisted out by a Coast Guard helicopter.
hazards.game_event_idea: Rounding a point, you see the next point is already awash behind you. Options: (A) Climb to a high ledge and wait (safe if you have warm layers and water; costs 5 hours; 10% chance you need a rescue if you climbed somewhere you cannot climb down). (B) Look for the red-and-black target sign of an overland trail (80% found if you carry the coastal map, 40% in fog without). (C) Wade back through the surge (20% success; failure = rescue ending in Gentle mode, worse in Classic mode).

hazards.name: Ozette River ford
hazards.season: Easiest late summer at low tide; may be impassable in shoulder seasons, winter and after heavy rain
hazards.real_world: Ford only at low tide. Shin-deep at a June 2026 low; rib-cage deep at mid-tide in August 2026 (everything in the hip pockets soaked).
hazards.game_event_idea: You reach the river at 2:30 pm, three hours after low. Options: (A) Ford now: chest-deep - 60% success with poles and unbuckled hip belt, 35% without; failure = soaked sleeping bag unless in a dry bag. (B) Camp on this side and ford at the 6 am low (only if your permit includes North/South Side of Ozette River - otherwise a ranger encounter). (C) Cross barefoot vs. in water shoes: barefoot adds 15% chance of a cut foot.

hazards.name: Falls Creek and Goodman Creek fords
hazards.season: Spring melt and fall-winter rain; Falls Creek also deepens with high tide
hazards.real_world: Goodman usually ankle-to-knee, Falls ankle-deep - but high tide pushes seawater up Falls Creek to thigh or waist depth, and both may be impossible in heavy rain.
hazards.game_event_idea: Falls Creek is roaring brown after a night of rain. Options: (A) Ford now (55% / 80% with poles; failure = swept a few yards, lose an item). (B) Look for the log crossing a ranger used (65%; slip = soaked). (C) Wait 3 hours for the tide to drop (costs time; may miss Diamond Rock window later).

hazards.name: Mosquito Creek ford
hazards.season: Year-round; deeper at high tide and after rain
hazards.real_world: Cross at mid-to-low tide: barefoot in sand at -1 ft, knee-deep at the mouth around +6 ft (2026).
hazards.game_event_idea: Ford barefoot (fast, 10% cut foot), in water shoes (safe, but you must have packed them), or in boots (wet feet for the 3.5 mi Hoh Head overland = blisters).

hazards.name: Rope and ladder overland trails
hazards.season: Year-round; slickest in rain
hazards.real_world: Overland trails are marked with round red-and-black targets (quartered discs nailed to trees; older guides call them 'lollipop' signs), are steep and muddy with minimal maintenance, and use cable ladders or fixed ropes; climb one at a time. NPS recommends leather gloves. In 2026 some entrances (Scott's Bluff, Goodman Creek) were marked only by hanging buoys. 2026: Scott's Bluff north ladder washed out (rope only); south of Point of the Arches a rope ended ~25 ft above the beach.
hazards.game_event_idea: The rope ends above a muddy drop. Options: (A) Hand-over-hand without gloves (barnacled rope: hands cut, -1 grip for the next climb). (B) Extend with the cord in your pack (needs 'cord' item; 95%). (C) Lower your pack first on the cord, then climb (needs cord; 90%; slow). (D) Go back and wait for a low tide to go around (if one exists).

hazards.name: Fog and hidden cliff edges on overland trails
hazards.season: Summer marine fog (Jul-Sep) and winter rain
hazards.real_world: NPS warns that thick vegetation hides cliff edges, which can be fatal. 2026 hikers lost the trail in brush on top of the 0.7 mi overland south of the Arches and found an eroding edge.
hazards.game_event_idea: Fog wraps the bluff and the trail splits in the salal. Options: (A) Follow the fresh-looking path (60%; 40% it ends at a crumbling edge - turn back, lose an hour). (B) Check the map/GPS (95% if you packed them and the battery is charged). (C) Wait for the fog to lift (lose time; tide window may close).

hazards.name: Sneaker waves and rolling drift logs
hazards.season: Year-round; most dangerous Oct-Apr with big swell
hazards.real_world: NPS: waves can move logs, which can crush and kill. The Coast Guard airlifted a 44-year-old hiker near the Hoh River mouth after the rising tide drove drift logs into him.
hazards.game_event_idea: A perfect photo spot: a giant log at the water's edge. Options: (A) Climb onto it (15% a surge rolls it: injury -> rescue ending). (B) Shoot from the high beach (safe). (C) Turn your back to the sea to pose (the narrator gently warns; 25% you get drenched and lose your camera).

hazards.name: Raccoons, bears and the bear-canister rule
hazards.season: Year-round; bears most visible spring-fall
hazards.real_world: Bear canisters are required for all food, garbage and scented items on the whole coast; hanging is not allowed because raccoons reach hung food. A habituated black bear roamed Cape Alava in July 2026 and lunged toward campers who crowded it; a sow with cubs foraged at Sand Point.
hazards.game_event_idea: At dusk you hear rustling: a raccoon has your trail mix. Options: (A) If you packed a canister and used it: nothing lost, a cute sketch. (B) If you left toothpaste in the tent: 50% a raccoon chews through the mesh. (C) No canister: lose 1-2 food days; a ranger may end the trip and fine you. With a bear: wave arms and shout 'hey bear' (90% it ambles off), or retreat and leave the canister 100 ft from the tent.

hazards.name: Ozette boardwalk: slick planks and old nails
hazards.season: Year-round; wet most of the time
hazards.real_world: NPS warns the three miles of boardwalk can be very slick and that soft-soled shoes grip better than stiff lug soles. Many boards are loose or rotten; hidden nails and spikes have injured hikers in sandals.
hazards.game_event_idea: Morning rain glazes the planks. Options: (A) Hurry in lugged boots (20% fall: bruised, slower). (B) Go slowly in soft-soled shoes (5%). (C) Sandals: 10% nail puncture -> first-aid kit check.

hazards.name: Dry creeks and brackish water
hazards.season: Late July-September
hazards.real_world: Wedding Rocks, Sand Point and South Sand Point sources typically dry up later in summer (NPS). Strawberry Point has no water. The Ozette River and some creeks turn brackish at high tide. All coastal water is tea-stained by tannins and carries giardia and cryptosporidium; iodine does not kill crypto.
hazards.game_event_idea: The creek at camp is a stagnant brown puddle. Options: (A) Filter it anyway (fine with a filter, 30% stomach trouble with iodine only). (B) Walk 1 mi back to a running creek (costs time). (C) Ration the 2 L you carried (thirst slows tomorrow).

hazards.name: Camping below the high-tide line
hazards.season: Biggest highs Nov-Jan (to ~11 ft at La Push in 2026), also spring-tide nights in summer
hazards.real_world: Late arrivals at busy beaches end up low on the sand; a 2025 party had to move camp as the tide crept up. Jefferson Cove's beach is inundated at high tide; a June 2026 party skipped it before a 10+ ft night tide.
hazards.game_event_idea: The only open spot is on smooth sand below a line of seaweed. Options: (A) Pitch here (if tonight's high > 8 ft: midnight flood, wet gear). (B) Read the wrack line and pitch above it in the logs (safe; uneven sleep). (C) Hike on to the next camp (time and tide check).

hazards.name: Pacific storms and hypothermia
hazards.season: October-April (also cold summer fog)
hazards.real_world: Wind and off-coast storms raise tides above predictions and make winter conditions especially hazardous (NPS). Rain can last for days; nothing dries.
hazards.game_event_idea: The marine forecast (zone PZZ150) calls for gale warnings tomorrow. Options: (A) Hunker in a forest site with a tarp (needs tarp; safe, lose a day). (B) Push on (storm surge adds ~1-2 ft to every tide gate; 40% a planned crossing closes). (C) Bail to the nearest trailhead.

hazards.name: Campfire rules, no-fire zone and 2026 burn ban
hazards.season: No-fire zone year-round; burn bans typically July-September
hazards.real_world: Beach fires only below the high-tide line, driftwood only, 10 ft from logs, no bigger than 3 ft. No fires from the Wedding Rocks headland to the headland north of Yellow Banks. In 2026 a Stage 2 ban prohibited all campfires park-wide from Aug 7; hikers at Shi Shi had to put out an abandoned bonfire.
hazards.game_event_idea: Your companions want a driftwood fire at Sand Point. Options: (A) Build it (ranger citation; the narrator sighs; score penalty). (B) Use your stove and tell stories (if you packed fuel). (C) Walk to a beach where fires are allowed - only if no ban is in force.

hazards.name: Stranded whale carcasses
hazards.season: Spring-summer gray whale migration; unusually many in 2026
hazards.real_world: In 2026 hikers reported gray and humpback carcasses at Toleak Point, near the Goodman Creek overland, Cape Alava, south of the Ozette River and north of Seafield Creek; one hiker counted 31 Washington whale deaths by August. Carcasses attract bears and vultures. Report strandings to NOAA's West Coast hotline (1-866-767-6114).
hazards.game_event_idea: A huge shape on the beach ahead, and a terrible smell. Options: (A) Detour upwind on the high beach and sketch from a distance (journal entry). (B) Camp nearby (bear visit chance doubles). (C) Note the location and report it at the trailhead (score bonus).

hazards.name: Ozette quota permits and fixed itineraries
hazards.season: Year-round; summer permits release April 15, 7 am PT
hazards.real_world: Camping from Yellow Banks to Point of the Arches is limited year-round (e.g., Seafield Creek 6 people/night, Yellow Banks 12, Cape Alava 43). No walk-up permits are held, and in quota areas you may not change your itinerary except in an emergency.
hazards.game_event_idea: Planning screen: Cape Alava is full for Saturday. Options: (A) Shift the trip to midweek. (B) Pick Sand Point instead. (C) Go without a permit (in-game ranger encounter: trip ends early, fine).

hazards.name: 2026 road closures: Mora Road and the Hoh River Bridge
hazards.season: Mora Road July 8 - Oct 15 (or Nov 9), 2026; Hoh River Bridge repair July 2026 - Sept 2028
hazards.real_world: Rialto Beach is unreachable by road during the Mora Road construction closure (pedestrians too). Full multi-day closures of the US 101 Hoh River Bridge in Sept-Oct 2026 cut Ruby Beach and Kalaloch off from Forks, forcing a 4+ hour detour.
hazards.game_event_idea: Drive phase: a 'ROAD CLOSED' barrier. Options: (A) Re-plan to a different trailhead (Second/Third Beach, Ozette). (B) Take the 4-hour detour (costs a day of the trip). (C) Wait for the noon reopening if it's the last closure day.

hazards.name: Kelp-slick boulders and sprained ankles
hazards.season: Year-round
hazards.real_world: Beach travel is arduous: hours of rock hopping over seaweed and barnacles at about 1 mph; 'pistol squats with a pack, over and over'. NPS warns algae-covered rocks and wet logs are slippery.
hazards.game_event_idea: Each boulder segment rolls a slip check: base 10%, -5% with trekking poles, -3% with gloves, +5% with heavy pack (> 35 lb), +10% in the rain. A slip costs time; a second slip in a day is a sprain (pace halves; consider a layover or bailing).

hazards.name: Earthquake and tsunami
hazards.season: Any time (rare)
hazards.real_world: The coast faces local (Cascadia subduction zone) and distant tsunamis; the last great Cascadia earthquake struck in January 1700. Remote beaches may get no official warning: strong shaking or a sudden drop or rise of the sea means walk inland and uphill at once, ideally to 50 ft or more.
hazards.game_event_idea: Rare event: the ground shakes for a long time. Options: (A) Head straight up the nearest overland trail or bluff (survive; trip ends, a quiet storybook epilogue). (B) Go down to look at the strange low water (Classic mode: game over; Gentle mode: a ranger's voice calls you back).

hazards.name: Cougar country
hazards.season: Year-round
hazards.real_world: A cougar-sighting notice was posted at the Third Beach trailhead in June 2026 and headland camps near Scott Creek were signed closed for wildlife activity; a 2017 party saw large feline tracks south of Shi Shi.
hazards.game_event_idea: Fresh big-cat tracks cross the sand at dawn. Options: (A) Keep kids/companions close and make noise (safe). (B) Follow the tracks for a sketch (Classic mode risk). (C) Leave early.

hazards.name: Sacred and protected places
hazards.season: Year-round
hazards.real_world: Tskawahyah (Cannonball) Island is always closed out of respect for the Makah. The Wedding Rocks petroglyphs are protected by federal law (ARPA); vandalism was reported in 2018. Camping is prohibited on the Ozette Indian Reservation strip between Cape Alava and the South Side of Ozette River camp.
hazards.game_event_idea: At low tide a sand bar leads to the island. Options: (A) Walk out (the narrator explains why not; score penalty, no sketch). (B) Sketch it from the beach (journal entry: the island at dusk).

hazards.name: Washed-up containers
hazards.season: Year-round, after storms
hazards.real_world: NPS: metal cylinders or containers that wash ashore may hold hazardous or explosive materials; do not touch, note markings and location, and report to a ranger.
hazards.game_event_idea: A rusty canister rolls in the surf. Options: (A) Kick it to see what's inside (Classic mode danger). (B) Note it and report it (score bonus).

wildlife_and_plants.name: Black bear
wildlife_and_plants.notes: Forages kelp and beach wrack at dawn and dusk; a habituated bear frequented Cape Alava in July 2026 and a sow with two cubs used Sand Point.
wildlife_and_plants.game_idea: Helper/advisor in the storybook (Bear tells the hiker to keep the canister closed); hazard if food is left out.
